newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Iraq news knocks oil price, chills OPEC.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq news knocks oil price, chills OPEC.

text.p: News that Iraq expects to resume oil exports under a U.N. oil-for-food pact within a week to 10 days sent the price of the barrel skidding on Tuesday.
The prospect, aired by Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Rasheed, directed a chill blast toward a conference that opens in Vienna on Wednesday of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

Delegates expect a fractious cartel simply to extend current production quotas until the end of the year. But quotas are being flouted in a way that has already undermined prices - down below $18 per barrel from $25 at the end of 1996.
The market had rallied this week, but less on prospects of stronger OPEC discipline than because of renewed tensions between Iraq and the United Nations.

It soon dropped by some 25 cents to around $17.75 on Tuesday after Iraq's Rasheed predicted an early end to delays to the next instalment of Iraqi sales under a pact with the U.N. that relaxes Gulf War sanctions.
"We expect to start exporting oil in the next week to 10 days and we don't anticipate any problems in discussions," Rasheed told a news conference during a pre-OPEC Madrid visit.
U.N. officials have also said Iraq is a week to 10 days from completing an aid distribution plan to restart sales.
Earlier, Saudi Arabia joined forces in Vienna with Gulf rival Iran to demand that other cartel members stop violating mandated OPEC production quotas.
But the Saudis appeared confident that rising demand for petroleum later this year would support the market, even under the pressure of OPEC output that is running at a 17-year high.
The ministers of OPEC kingpin Saudi Arabia and Iran, the cartel's second biggest producer, both spoke to lobby reporters ahead of the OPEC conference.
The likely outcome will be a decision to freeze current quotas for six months from June 30, several ministers said.
Saudi Arabia's Ali Naimi declared that "a rollover is good if everyone adheres to their quota...We would like everyone to honour their commitments".
But he added that markets could support current actual OPEC production, assessed by the Saudis at up to two million barrels daily in excess of the mandated ceiling of 25.03 million.
"Demand is good. There is no reason for prices to go lower," he told reporters.
Iran's minister, Gholamreza Aghazadeh, was blunt in saying that something had to be done about discipline. "Any decision without stopping the violations does not pay," he said.

Delegates said privately that apart from giving a closed session tongue-lashing to the Venezuelan minister, Erwin Arrieta, and other alleged violators, it was hard to see what the rest of OPEC could do to police better quota discipline.
Petroleos de Venezuela, the Venezuelan state oil company, has said that OPEC ought to abandon quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
Arrieta, assessed by monitors to be 800,000 barrels above his quota, says he will not actually demand that quotas be abolished, but that he would like to air ideas for change.
He said that "revenue is the key".
-- Vienna newsroom +431 713 2002
